groups.title: Context API internals and when it causes re-renders
groups.question: Your app keeps the user, theme and a complex shopping cart in one React Context, and typing in the search box makes the whole app re-render. Explain why that happens and how you'd restructure the state, including the cart's update logic.

followUps.How Context propagates values and trigge: Why does a component that only reads the theme re-render when the cart changes, and how would you fix it?
followUps.useReducer for state with multiple relat: Why would useReducer suit the cart better than several useState calls?

evidence.text: Every component that uses a context re-renders when the context value changes, even if it only uses part of it.
Passing a new object as the value on every render counts as a change too.
Splitting contexts by what changes together, or memoizing the value, limits the re-renders to components that need them.

notEnough: Only saying Context causes re-renders without explaining which components and why.

evidence.text: useReducer keeps related values in one state and computes the next state in a reducer function from the current state and an action.
All the update rules live in one place, which keeps fields consistent with each other.
The reducer is a pure function, so it can be tested without rendering anything.

notEnough: Only saying useReducer is for complex state without explaining actions and the reducer.

groups.title: React Router v6 rendering model
groups.question: Your dashboard has a shared sidebar layout with several pages, and one page renders a big chart that recalculates on every keystroke elsewhere on the page. Explain how the pages render inside the layout and how you'd decide whether memoization fixes the slow chart.

followUps.Nested routes and the Outlet component f: How does the dashboard layout know where to render the current child page?
followUps.useMemo and useCallback: when memoizatio: When does useMemo or useCallback actually help, and when does it just add cost?

evidence.text: A parent route renders the shared layout, and the child routes are defined inside it.
The parent places an Outlet where the matched child route renders, so the layout stays and only the inner page changes.

notEnough: Only saying use nested routes and Outlet without explaining what renders where.

evidence.text: useMemo keeps a computed value and useCallback keeps a function between renders until their dependencies change.
They help for expensive calculations, or when a stable reference stops a memoized child or an effect from running again.
Elsewhere they add comparison work for no gain, so they're added after a profiler shows a real problem.

notEnough: Only saying useMemo makes things faster without saying when.

misconceptions.text: Says every value and function should be wrapped in useMemo or useCallback.

groups.title: Custom hooks for reusable stateful logic
groups.question: Three pages in your app repeat the same fetch-with-loading-and-error logic, and the first load downloads the code for every page, including the admin area. Explain how you'd remove the duplication and make the first load smaller.

followUps.Extracting stateful logic into custom ho: What makes a function a custom hook, and does sharing a hook share the state between components?
followUps.Code splitting with React.lazy and Suspe: How do React.lazy and Suspense change when the admin page's code is downloaded, and what does the user see meanwhile?

evidence.text: A custom hook is a function whose name starts with use and that calls other hooks, so stateful logic can be reused.
Each component that calls the hook gets its own state; the logic is shared, not the data.

notEnough: Only saying put it in a custom hook without saying what a hook is or what it shares.

misconceptions.text: Says components that use the same custom hook share the same state.

evidence.text: React.lazy with a dynamic import puts the component in a separate chunk that downloads only when it is first rendered.
Suspense shows a fallback, like a spinner, while that chunk loads.
The first page load downloads less code, so the app becomes usable sooner.

notEnough: Only saying use lazy loading without explaining when the code is downloaded.

groups.title: React Router navigation APIs
groups.question: Your app has a post page at /posts/:id with filters in the URL like ?sort=new, and a settings page only logged-in users may open. Explain how the page reads the id and filters, how you send users somewhere after an action, and how you keep logged-out users away from settings.

followUps.useNavigate, useParams, and useSearchPar: Why keep the sort filter in the URL with useSearchParams instead of in component state?
followUps.Protected routes using wrapper component: How would a protected route wrapper decide what to render, and where does it get the auth state from?

evidence.text: useParams reads dynamic segments of the URL, like the id in /posts/:id.
useSearchParams reads and updates the query string, so filters survive a reload and can be shared as a link.
useNavigate sends the user to another route from code, for example after saving a form.

notEnough: Only listing the hook names without saying what each one reads or does.

evidence.text: A wrapper component reads the auth state, for example from context, and renders the protected page only for logged-in users.
Otherwise it redirects to the login page, for example with Navigate.
The API still has to check auth itself, because hiding a route in the browser doesn't protect the data.

notEnough: Only saying use a protected route without explaining the check and the redirect.

misconceptions.text: Says hiding a route in React is enough to keep the data secure.
